quick_english: Therefore, standing between knowledge and ignorance, you are instructed by the holy Lord. The holy Lord said: your inner self is struck by humanity; overcome by grief and delusion, you are seized by pity; seeing kinsmen who have approached the mouth of death, what obstacle is yours? They have entered it themselves.

quick_english: You grieve for what should not be grieved and do not speak like a wise person; learned ones do not grieve for the departed or the living. It is impossible to grieve for the body, since it is always perishable; and you grieve for the self, which is not worthy of grief. No one, whether dead or living, is to be grieved; for the self is indestructible, moving through various bodies, so what grief-worthiness is there? Nor is there grief-worthiness in the transfer of bodies; otherwise grief-worthiness would arise even in youth and so on.

quick_english: This Self is unmanifest, inconceivable, and unmodifiable; therefore, having known it, one should not grieve. No weapon or other cause can destroy him, since he is of one conscious nature, independent, partless, and free, and cannot be destroyed by another nature, dependence, destruction of parts, or division. Nor is his going to another body something new: even while embodied he always goes to another body, and therefore he is connected. Since a body does not remain even for a moment, having known this Self thus, one should not grieve.

quick_english: By chance such war arrives with heaven's gate opened; meritorious kshatriyas obtain it, Partha. Even desire-filled kshatriyas should not abandon such war because it causes heaven; how much less one to whom such knowledge is taught. The verse's purport is not merely ending in heaven.

quick_english: Thus fools speak this flowery speech, attached to Vedic debate, O Partha, claiming nothing else exists.
Desire-natured, heaven-focused, desiring fruits of birth and action, full of special rites, they follow paths toward enjoyment and power.

For minds stolen by that speech, resolute understanding is not given in concentration; desire-craving speakers praise flowery Vedic speech filled with future heaven-fruit, desire fruit from action, and even with resolute understanding are not fit for concentration because of fruit-certainty; this is the purport of the three verses.

quick_english: Therefore the Vedas concern the three strands; be beyond them, Arjuna, beyond pairs, established in constant being, free from acquisition and security, self-possessed. If this were Veda-criticism, the matter of doing battle would be obstructed, for lack of certainty of own duty without Veda; but for those whose desire for fruit has fallen away, the Vedas are not binders.

Attachment through absence of action is firm-grasp false knowing, to be abandoned indeed.

quick_english: One whose undertakings are free from desire-bonds is the wise renouncer; longing binds.
cite_parts: tyāge yasya hutaṃ  sarvaṃ sa tyāgī sa ca buddhimān
yasya sarve vyāpārā āśīrūpeṇa bandhanena na yuktāḥ

quick_english: Action is far inferior to yoga of wisdom; seek refuge in intellect, for wretched fruit-causers remain distant.
cite_parts: atastādṛśyāṃ buddhau śaraṇamanviccha-prārthayasva yena sā  buddhirlabhyate

quick_english: Joined to intellect, one abandons both good and bad deeds; yoga is skill in actions.
cite_parts: tasmāt-yathāhi  sukṛttaduṣkṛte naśyatastathākaraṇameva paramaṃ kauśalamiti  bhāvaḥ

quick_english: Wise ones, abandoning action-born fruit, are freed from birth-bond and attain the unailing state.
cite_parts: karmajaṃ buddhiyuktā hi phalaṃ tyaktvā manīṣiṇaḥ
yogabuddhiyuktāḥ karmaṇāṃ phalaṃ tyaktvā janmabandhaṃ  tyajantibrahmasattāmavāpnuvanti

quick_english: When your intellect crosses the delusion-thicket, then you will go to weariness of what is to be heard and heard.
cite_parts: tadā gantāsi nirvedaṃ  śrotavyasya śrutasya ca

quick_english: When your intellect stands unmoving in samadhi, you will attain yoga; then recognition becomes clear and dispassion follows.
cite_parts: tatra ca yogabuddhiprāptyavasare va sphuṭamevedamabhijñānam  śrotavyasya śrutasyābhilaṣyamāṇasya ca āgamasya ubhayasyāpi  nirvedabhāktvam
anena  cedamuktam-avidyāpadanipatitapramātranugrāhakaśāstraśravaṇasaṃsk  āra-vipralambhamahimā ayaṃ - yattavāsthāne  kulakṣayādidoṣadarśanam tattu tathā śāsanabahumānavigalane  vigaliṣyatīti

quick_english: Arjuna asks what speech, sitting, and going characterize steady wisdom in samadhi.
cite_parts: arjuna uvāca   sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhisthasya keśava
sthiradhīḥ  kiṃ prabhāṣeta kimāsīta vrajecca kim

yadā sthāsyati buddhiḥ-ityanena vacasā samādhisthasya yogino yaḥ  sthitaprajñaśabdastatra vācaka uktastasya kā bhāṣā-kiṃ  pravṛttinimittaṃ bhāṣyate yena nimittena śabdairartha iti kṛtvā  yoginaḥ sthitaprajñaśabdaḥ kiṃ rūḍhyā vācako'nvarthatayā vā  iti ekaḥ praśnaḥ
yadyapi rūḍhau śaṅkaiva nāsti  tathāpyanvarthatāṃ labdhāmapi svarūpalakṣaṇanimittanirūpaṇena  sphuṭīkartumeṣa praśnaḥ
sthiradhīriti  śabdapadārthako'rthapadārthakaśca tatra sthiradhīśabdaḥ kiṃ  prayogalakṣaṇamevārthamāha āho tapasvinamapi iti dvitīyaḥ  praśnaḥ
sa ca sthiradhīryogī kimāsīt-kimabhyasyet-kvāsya  sthairyaṃ syāt iti tṛtīyaḥ

quick_english: When one abandons all desires and is content in the self, steady wisdom is declared.
cite_parts: etadeva praśnacatuṣṭayaṃ krameṇa nirṇīyate śrībhagavatā   śrī bhagavānuvāca   prajahāti yadā kāmānsarvānpārtha manogatān
rūḍhiśca nityamātmarūḍhitve sati viṣayavikṣepakṛtasya  kāmarūpasya bhramasya nivṛttatvāt yogino yaḥ  sthitaprajña-śabdo'nvarthaḥ sa cetthaṃyukta ityekaḥ praśno  nirṇītaḥ

quick_english: Unagitated in suffering, desireless in pleasure, free from attachment, fear, and anger, such a sage is steady-minded.
cite_parts: sukhaduḥkhayoryasya rāgadveṣarahitā vṛttiḥ sa munireva  sthiraprajño nānyaḥ

quick_english: Fitting, because one unattached everywhere, obtaining good or bad, neither rejoices nor hates, and wisdom is established.
cite_parts: yuktaṃ caitat yataḥ   yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehastattatprāpya śubhāśubham
nābhinandati na  dveṣṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā

quick_english: When one withdraws the senses from objects like a tortoise, steady wisdom is declared.
cite_parts: na cāsya pācakavadyogarūḍhitvam yadā yadā kilāyamindriyāṇi  saṃharate-ātmanyeva kūrma ivāṅgāni kroḍīkaroti viṣayibhyo  viṣayānnivārya tadā tadā sthiraprajñaḥ
yadvā-indriyārthebhyaḥ prabhṛti indriyāṇi ātmani  saṃharate-viṣayendriyādikaṃ sarvamātmasātkaroti
nanu tapasvino'pi kathaṃ sthiraprajñaśabdo na pravartate ? ucyate-

quick_english: Objects withdraw from one who fasts, but taste remains; seeing the supreme removes that residue, so only the yogin is steady in wisdom.
cite_parts: yadyapi āhāryaiḥ-rūpādibhirviṣayaiḥ saṃbandho'sya nāsti  tathāpi tasya viṣayā antaḥkaraṇagatamuparāgalakṣaṇaṃ rasaṃ  varjayitvā nivartante
yoginastu  parameśvaradarśanāduparāgo na bhavati anyasya tu tapasvino nāsau  nivartate

quick_english: Even a wise person's mind is seized by turbulent senses, so the yogin must conquer the mind.
cite_parts: yat-yasmāt tasyāpi-tapasvino mana indriyairhiyate athavā  yattasya-sayatnasyāpi
yoginā ca mana eva jetavyam iti dvitīyo  nirṇītaḥ

quick_english: Having restrained the senses by mind, one should sit devoted to me; wisdom is established when senses are controlled.
cite_parts: tāni saṃyamya manasā yukta āsīta matparaḥ
vaśe hi  yasyendriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā
ya evaṃ manasā indriyāṇi niyamayati natu apravṛttyā sa eva  sthiraprajñaḥ
sa ca matpara evāsīta-māmeva cidātmānaṃ  parameśvaraṃ abhyasyet

quick_english: For one meditating on objects, attachment arises; from attachment desire, and from desire anger.
Anger leads to delusion, memory confusion, intellect destruction, and ruin; mere renunciation ends in grasping, so it is not the means for steady wisdom.
cite_parts: dhyānakāla eva ca saṅgādaya upajāyante-ityanupāyo  viṣayatyāgaḥ sthiraprajñasya

quick_english: Freed from attachment and aversion, moving through objects with controlled senses, the self-controlled one attains serenity.
In calmness, loss of all sorrows arises for him; indeed quickly the intellect of the clear-minded one becomes established.
There is no intellect for the unyoked one, nor meditation for the unyoked one, nor peace for the unpeaceful one; whence happiness?
Indeed, of the roaming senses, the mind that follows them carries away his wisdom, as wind carries a boat on water.

tokens.grounds: genitive plural masculine participle of car

quick_english: Therefore, O mighty-armed one, whose senses are wholly restrained from sense-objects, his wisdom is established; but one who controls the mind, even while serving objects, is not overwhelmed by waves of anger and the like; thus he alone is the steady-wisdom yogi—this is the purport.
cite_parts: yastu manaso niyāmakaḥ sa viṣayānsevamāno'pi na  krodhādikallolairabhibhūyate iti sa eva sthiraprajño yogī-iti  tātparyam

quick_english: The yogi, though performing all practical dealings, is transcendent; the supreme Lord, having summarized his own nature, tells it: the night of all beings is the sage's waking; the night in which beings wake is the sage's night; how is this maya, the deluding night of all beings, to be abandoned? In the state where the world wakes and performs various activities, that is the sage's night, because he is unawakened to practical dealing. This is said: this maya indeed has deluding nature, name-and-form, and appearance of dependence on pleasure; there the world, without touching her original own-nature, sits bound in memory in the second form. The yogi, however, is opposite: he sees her deluding nature for uprooting it, and does not regard dependence on pleasure; seeing rightly, the knower disregards dependence on pleasure through destruction of false knowledge. See indeed, that is night—wonder! In knowledge the yogi attends where all are deluded; in ignorance, however, where a person is unawakened, there he is awakened—also wonder.
cite_parts: yogī ca sarvavyavahārān kurvāṇo'pi lokottaraḥ-iti nirūpayatā  parameśvareṇa saṃkṣipyāsya svarūpaṃ kathyate   yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṃ tasyāṃ jāgarti saṃyamī
yasyāṃ  jāgrati bhūtāni sā rātriḥ paśyato muneḥ
yā sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ niśā-mohanī māyā tasyāṃ  munirjāgarti-kathamiyaṃ heyeti
yasyāṃ ca daśāyāṃ loko  jāgarti-nānāvidhāṃ ceṣṭāṃ kurute sā muneḥ rātriḥ yato'sau  vyavahāraṃ pratyabuddhaḥ
etaduktaṃ bhavati-yeyaṃ māyā khalu  tasyā mohakatvaṃ nāmarūpaṃ sukhatantratābhāsanaṃ ca
tatra-lokaḥ prācyaṃ svarūpamasyā aparāmṛśyaiva dvitīyasminrūpe  nibaddhasmṛtirāste
yogī tu tadviparītastadīyaṃ mohakatvaṃ  tadunmūlanāya paśyati sukhatantratāṃ tu nādriyate
vidyāyāṃ cāvadhatte yogī yatra  sarvo vimūḍhaḥ
avidyāyāṃ tvabuddhaḥ yatra janaḥ  prabuddhaḥ-ityapi citram

quick_english: Therefore indeed, just as waters enter the ocean that is being filled yet remains immovably established, so all desires enter him; he attains peace, not the desire-desiring one. The yogi does not run outward even for desire's sake; but by sense-nature, objects entering after him do not make waves, like river currents into the ocean. Thus the third is decided.
cite_parts: ata eva   āpūryamāṇamacalapratiṣṭhaṃ samudramāpaḥ praviśanti yadvat
tadvatkāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve sa śāntimāpnoti na kāmakāmī
yogī na kāmārthaṃ bahirdhāvati api tvindriyadharmatayā
taṃ  viṣayā anupraviśanto na taraṅgayanti nadīvegā ivodadhim

quick_english: Having abandoned all desires, the desireless, selfless, egoless man walks and attains peace; that yogi, through renunciation of all desires, reaches liberation in the form of peace.

This is the brahmic state, Partha; having reached it one is not deluded, and even at the end one reaches brahma-nirvana. This brahma-being, in which even a moment's stability, once obtained, leads from body-breaking to supreme brahman, is thus the resolution of the four questions; auspicious.
cite_parts: eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha naināṃ prāpya vimuhyati
eṣāsau brahmasattā yasyāṃ kṣaṇamātraṃ sthitvā-avasthitiṃ  prāpya śarīrabhedāt paramaṃ brahmāpnoti iti praśnacatuṣṭayaṃ  nirṇītamiti śivam

quick_english: Here is the summary verse: ah, indeed the mind's wondrous course ascends by abandonment; taking refuge in objects, one should abandon them. Thus in the Gita-meaning-gathering composed by Abhinavagupta, the second chapter.
cite_parts: atra saṃgrahaślokaḥ   aho nu cetasaścitrā gatistyāgena yatkila
